entries.title: The brigade de cuisine
entries.summary: The brigade de cuisine is the kitchen's chain of command, from the chef de cuisine down to the commis and the plongeur. It tells every cook what they own, who they answer to and how a whole kitchen moves as one.
entries.guest: In a classical kitchen the chef leads a brigade, with a sous chef as second and a cook in charge of each station, so every part of your plate has an owner.

paras: Brigade de cuisine (bree-GAHD duh kwee-ZEEN) means kitchen brigade: a team organised like a small army, where every job has one owner and every owner answers to one person. When a ticket arrives nobody wonders who is cooking the fish or making the sauce, and that clarity lets a crowded, hot kitchen work fast without collisions. For a new cook it settles the first question, who do I answer to. For a new server it explains the kitchen on the other side of the pass, the counter where finished plates leave.

The chef de cuisine (shef duh kwee-ZEEN), the head of the kitchen, sets the menu and the standards, runs the team and carries the result; chef simply means chief. The sous chef (SOO shef), the under chef, is second in command: runs the kitchen day to day, trains the cooks and takes over when the chef is away. A chef de partie (shef duh par-TEE) owns one station and the cooks on it. A demi-chef de partie is that station chef's deputy, or runs a small station alone.

The commis (koh-MEE) is a junior cook who learns one station at a time under its chef de partie. The apprenti (ah-prahn-TEE) is an apprentice, still in training. The plongeur (plohn-ZHUR), from plonger, to plunge, washes the pots, pans and plates, and without clean pans service stops within minutes. A new cook answers first to the chef de partie of the station, and goes further up the line only when sent. Going over your station chef's head breaks the very chain that keeps service calm.

The dining room, the front of house, has a brigade of its own, just as the kitchen is the back of house. The maître d'hôtel (MAY-truh doh-TEL), or maître d', runs the room. The chef de rang (shef duh RAHN) runs a section of tables, as an American captain does. The commis de rang carries plates, clears and learns the section, and the sommelier (suh-mul-YAY) looks after the wine. Between the two brigades stands the aboyeur (ah-bwah-YUR), the barker, from aboyer, to bark, who calls the orders to the stations and the plates to the waiters: the job an American kitchen calls expediting.

An American kitchen keeps the logic under plainer names: an executive chef, often over more than one kitchen, a chef de cuisine running this one, sous chefs, line cooks on the stations, prep cooks making the mise en place, the prepared ingredients, and dishwashers in the plongeur's place. The World Table borrows the ladder for its four levels, Commis, Chef de Partie, Sous Chef and Chef, each a rank earned by work, as in a kitchen.

Kitchens ran by rank long before the brigade had a name, but the system as cooks know it is credited to Auguste Escoffier (es-koff-ee-AY). He joined the hotelier César Ritz at the Savoy in London in 1890, Ritz running the hotel and Escoffier its kitchens, then set up the kitchens of the Ritz in Paris in 1898. His aim was to end duplicated effort: each station made its element for everyone, so a single plate drew on several stations working at the same moment, brought together at the pass.

Brennan's own story shows how far the ladder runs. The house records that Lazone Randolph began here as a dishwasher in 1965 and became executive chef in 2005, and that Kris Padalino, executive chef since June 2025, spent eight years in this kitchen as pastry chef and executive sous chef first. The dining room has captains; who carves, who flames and how the floor is organised on a given night are questions for lineup, the short meeting before service.

Respect for every rank is the habit of a good kitchen: please and thank you at full speed, the plongeur called by name, your own mess cleared before you leave a station. When a guest asks who cooked their dinner, the true answer is the brigade: the chef's standards, and a cook at each station who owns one part of the plate.

questions.q: What does the title sous chef mean?

distractors: The sauce chef, in charge of sauces
The head of the dining room
The cook who covers any station

questions.answer: The chef de partie of the fish station
distractors: The executive chef, directly
The chef de partie of the sauce station
The aboyeur at the pass

questions.q: Which rank of the brigade washes the pots, pans and plates?
questions.answer: The plongeur
distractors: The commis de rang
The apprenti
The aboyeur
questions.why: Plongeur comes from plonger, to plunge. The commis de rang works in the dining room, the apprenti is an apprentice cook and the aboyeur calls the orders.

questions.answer: Chef de rang
distractors: Commis de rang
Sommelier
Maître d'hôtel
questions.why: The chef de rang runs a section of tables, as a captain does; the maître d'hôtel runs the whole room, the commis de rang assists and the sommelier handles wine.

questions.q: What is the aboyeur's job in the classical brigade?

Pouring and decanting the wine at the table

entries.title: The stations
entries.summary: A station, or partie, is one part of the kitchen with one job: sauces, fish, roasts, grill, fryer, vegetables, cold food, pastry. Knowing which station cooks what tells a cook where to stand and a server why a plate may be running late.
entries.guest: In a classical kitchen each part of a plate has its own station: the steak from the grill, the potatoes from the fryer, the vegetables from another cook, joined at the last moment.

paras: A station is a cook's territory: the stove, the tools, the prepared ingredients and the dishes that one cook, or one small team, owns for the night. The French word is partie, a part, which is why its leader is a chef de partie. Escoffier's brigade divided the kitchen so that every station could work at once on its own element of a plate. Learn the stations and the menu reads as a map: each dish is a set of parts, and each part has a home.

The saucier (soh-SYAY) makes the sauces and the sautéed dishes, cooked to order in a pan with their sauce. It was the senior station of the classical kitchen, because sauce was the heart of French cooking and the work leaves no margin: a reduction or a butter sauce finished at the last minute, every minute of service. In smaller kitchens the saucier usually takes the fish as well.

The poissonnier (pwah-sun-YAY) cooks the fish and seafood, and often prepares them too. The rôtisseur (roh-tee-SUR) roasts meat and poultry and makes their jus, the roasting juices served with them. The grillardin (gree-yar-DAN) works the grill and the friturier (free-too-RYAY) the fryer; in the classical scheme both work under the rôtisseur, and in a smaller kitchen the rôtisseur does both jobs.

The entremetier (ahn-truh-meh-TYAY) cooks the vegetables, soups, eggs and starches such as potatoes, rice and pasta. In the largest kitchens the job splits: a potager (poh-tah-ZHAY) makes the soups and a légumier (lay-goo-MYAY) the vegetables, both under the entremetier.

The garde manger (gard mahn-ZHAY), whose name means keeper of the food, runs the cold kitchen: salads, terrines (seasoned meat, fish or vegetable mixtures cooked in a mould and served cold), cold sauces such as mayonnaise and the cold starters. The boucher (boo-SHAY) breaks meat and poultry down into portions for the other stations. The pâtissier (pah-tee-SYAY) makes the pastry and desserts, and the boulanger (boo-lahn-ZHAY) bakes the bread. The tournant (toor-NAHN), the roundsman, covers any station on another cook's night off, so must know them all.

An American restaurant keeps the stations under plainer names along the hot line, the row of stoves, grills and fryers facing the pass. Sauté is the saucier's heir: pans, sauces and often the fish. Grill takes the steaks, chops and anything marked over the fire. Fry runs the fryers. Cold, also called pantry, plates the salads and cold starters, the garde manger's work. Pastry often works apart, in a room of its own. Expo, short for expediter, stands at the pass and calls the line, and has an entry of its own. A small kitchen may fold three of these stations into one cook.

Brennan's menus show how much fry work one kitchen can carry. The house lists popcorn shrimp, fried Gulf shrimp, fried pickles, crispy artichokes and a fried Cornish hen among its fried dishes, and its guide sends every question about coatings, shared fryers or the oil to the kitchen, every time. For fish, the guide's habit is to know today's Gulf fish and how it is cooked, confirmed at lineup, the short meeting before service.

For a server, the stations explain the kitchen's rhythm. A table's plates leave together only when every station on the ticket is ready, so one late table usually means one station is behind: a grill full of steaks, a fryer coming back to heat. Ask the pass, not the cook, and give the guest a plain answer about the wait.

brennans.how: Popcorn shrimp are fry station work: classically dredged in seasoned flour or a light batter and fried quickly until golden. Every question about the coating, a shared fryer or the oil goes to the kitchen.
Sautéing is the saucier's craft: the children's Sautéed Gulf Fish is cooked quickly in a little hot fat in a wide pan and turned once. Know today's fish and its preparation at lineup.

entries.title: Calls on the line
entries.say: As it reads: calls on the line.
entries.summary: Calls are the short spoken words a kitchen runs on: oui chef, heard, behind, hot, fire, all day, eighty-six. Each says one thing fast and each is answered, so orders are heard and bodies and blades stay out of harm.
entries.guest: I'm sorry, the kitchen has just run out of that dish tonight. May I suggest something close to it?

paras: A kitchen in service is loud, hot and fast, and nobody has time for a full sentence. Calls are the short, fixed words that carry the essentials: an order heard, a body moving behind you, a pan too hot to touch, a dish run out. Every cook learns the same words, so they mean the same thing in every mouth, and every call is answered. As far as the kitchen knows, a call that is not answered was not heard.

Oui, chef, or yes, chef, is the answer to an instruction from the chef or the pass, the counter where finished plates leave the kitchen. It does not mean agreement; it means I heard it and I am on it. Heard does the same job in many American kitchens: the expediter, who runs the pass, calls an order and the station answers heard. In a French kitchen a new order may be announced with ça marche (sah MARSH), literally it walks: it is going, start it. Cooks say it back to mean got it, it's going.

Fire means cook it now: fire table twelve tells each station to start that table's next course. Ordering, in many kitchens, reads a new ticket aloud so stations can get ready before the fire. All day is the running total across every open ticket: four filets all day means four to cook in all. On the fly means as fast as possible, ahead of the queue, usually for a missed or dropped plate. Walking in warns that a party or a large order has just arrived. In the window means plates are up at the pass, waiting to go. Hands, called from the pass, means plates are ready and someone must carry them now.

Eighty-six means out: eighty-six the soup means no more soup tonight. The cook calls it to the pass the moment the last portion goes, and the servers must hear it before they sell another. Where the phrase came from is disputed, and no single story is proven. In the weeds means a station is overwhelmed and falling behind. Saying so early is a strength, not a confession: help can be sent only to a cook who asks.

Some calls exist, by long kitchen custom, to prevent injuries. Behind means someone is passing at your back: hold still, and do not step back or turn suddenly. Corner warns that someone is coming round a blind corner. Hot means a hot pan, tray or pot is moving: give way, and never grab what has just been set down. Sharp means a knife is being carried, point down and close to the leg. Call loudly, every time, even in a quiet kitchen: the habit works only if it never lapses.

The common failures are silence and assumption. A cook who does not answer leaves the pass guessing, so the call comes again, louder, while the table waits. A cook who moves without calling behind or hot invites a burn or a spill. A server who sells a dish after it has been eighty-sixed promises the guest something the kitchen cannot make. The fix is always the same: call it, answer it, and repeat the essential part back, so fire table twelve is met with heard, twelve.

Servers hear these calls too and answer them like cooks. When the kitchen eighty-sixes a dish, it comes off the server's list at once, and the guest hears it in plain English, never kitchen slang: the kitchen has run out of that tonight, and here is something close. Hands from the pass means go now if your hands are free, and a server crossing the kitchen calls behind and hot like everyone else.

faults.cause: The cook did not hear it, or heard it and stayed silent.
faults.fix: Answer every call with heard or oui, chef, and repeat the table or the item back.

faults.fault: A collision or a burn at someone's back
faults.cause: A cook moved behind another, or carried a hot pan, without calling.
faults.fix: Call behind, hot or sharp loudly every time, even in a quiet kitchen.

faults.fault: A dish sold after it has run out
faults.cause: The eighty-six never reached the floor, or a server missed it.
faults.fix: Call it to the pass the moment the last portion goes; every server strikes it at once.

faults.cause: A cook too proud or too busy to say in the weeds.
faults.fix: Say it early, so the sous chef can send help before the tickets pile up.

entries.title: The pass and expediting
entries.say: As it reads: the pass and expediting.
entries.summary: The pass is the counter between kitchen and dining room where every plate is checked before it goes. The expediter runs it, reading tickets, firing courses and timing each table so its plates leave together, hot and right.
entries.guest: The pass is where the kitchen checks each plate before it comes out, so a table's dishes can arrive together, as the cooks mean them to be.

paras: The pass is the counter, often under heat lamps, between the hot line and the dining room. Cooks set finished plates on one side and servers collect them from the other. It is the kitchen's last checkpoint: nothing reaches a guest without crossing it, so whoever stands there sees every plate the kitchen sends. In the classical brigade the aboyeur called the orders there, with the chef or the sous chef beside him checking the plates; in many American kitchens the expediter, called expo, does both jobs.

The expediter, the aboyeur of the old brigade, owns the tickets. As each order arrives the expediter reads it to the line so the stations can prepare, then fires each course when the table is ready for it: soup bowls cleared, fire the mains. Plates are called for by table, collected as they come up and checked one by one against the ticket: the right dish, cooked as ordered, with its sauce and garnish, hot, with a clean rim and nothing missing.

Timing is the craft. A table's plates should leave together, so the expediter counts back from the slowest dish: if the steak takes twelve minutes with its rest and the fish six, the steak is fired first and the fish six minutes later, and both reach the pass at the same moment. Hot food goes out hot, on warm plates. A sauce that has sat long enough to form a skin goes back for fresh, because a plate that dies under the lamp reaches the guest worse.

A server at the pass has one job: carry the plates as they leave, quickly and correctly. Arrive with hands free, know the table and its seat numbers so each guest gets their plate without being asked who had the fish, and hold each plate from underneath, the thumb flat on the outer edge of the rim and pointing outwards, never across the rim the cook has just wiped or near the food. Check the ticket as you lift. If a table is not ready, a guest away or menus still open, tell the expediter before the course is fired, not after.

A refire is a dish cooked again, and a remake one rebuilt, usually because it came back from the table or failed the check: a steak over or under, a cold plate, the wrong order. Bring a problem to the pass calmly and plainly: table, seat, dish, what is wrong and what the guest would like. The expediter fires the replacement first, ahead of the queue, and decides whether the rest of the table waits or eats. Blame waits until after service; the guest's dinner cannot.

A plate for a guest with an allergy is handled differently by the kitchen from the moment the ticket is written. The server writes the need on the ticket the way the house requires, and the kitchen decides what the dish can be. At the pass that allergy plate is flagged, checked against the ticket with the kitchen and carried separately: alone, never stacked with other plates or handed to whoever is free, straight to its seat. The full conversation with the guest has its own entry; at the pass, every allergy question goes to the kitchen.

At Brennan's the house guide is plain: guests note dietary needs at the reservation, the server writes them on the ticket, and the kitchen clears every choice, because the kitchen, not the server, says what a dish can do. Its practice scenarios add: flag the ticket and tell the captain.

faults.fault: A table's plates arriving minutes apart
faults.cause: Courses fired without counting back from the slowest dish.
faults.fix: Fire the longest cook first, so every plate reaches the pass at the same moment.

faults.fault: A cold plate or a skinned sauce
faults.cause: The plate waited under the lamp for a server or for a missing dish.
faults.fix: Servers arrive with free hands; a plate that has died at the pass goes back for fresh.

faults.fault: The wrong plate at the wrong seat
faults.cause: No seat numbers, so the server had to ask the table who had what.
faults.fix: Know the table and seat numbers at the pass, and check the ticket as you lift.

faults.fault: A remake that starts an argument
faults.cause: The problem was brought to the pass in anger, or without the details.
faults.fix: Give table, seat, dish and fault calmly, and settle any blame after service.

faults.fault: A flagged plate mixed up with others
faults.cause: It was carried in a stack, or handed to whoever was free.
faults.fix: Check it with the kitchen at the pass and carry it alone, straight to its seat.

cards.front: What is the pass?
cards.back: The counter between the hot line and the dining room where finished plates are checked and handed to servers; nothing reaches a guest without crossing it.

cards.front: What does the expediter do?
cards.back: Reads the tickets to the line, fires each course when the table is ready, calls for the plates and checks every one before it leaves.

cards.front: Who runs the pass in a classical brigade, and who in many American kitchens?
cards.back: In the classical brigade the aboyeur calls the orders while the chef or sous chef checks the plates; in many American kitchens the expediter, called expo, does both.

cards.front: What does the expediter check on every plate?
cards.back: The right dish for the ticket, cooked as ordered, with its sauce and garnish, hot, with a clean rim and nothing missing.

cards.front: How does the expediter make a table's plates arrive together?
cards.back: By counting back from the slowest dish: the longest cook is fired first, so every plate reaches the pass at the same moment.

cards.front: What happens to a plate that has sat too long at the pass?
cards.back: It goes back. Hot food must go out hot, and a sauce that has formed a skin is replaced with fresh.

cards.front: What does a server bring to the pass?
cards.back: Free hands and the table's seat numbers, and a check of the ticket as the plates are lifted.

cards.front: Where does a server's thumb go when carrying a plate, and why?
cards.back: Flat at the outer edge of the rim, pointing outwards, never across the rim or near the food: the cook has just wiped it, and a print there is the last thing a guest should see.

cards.front: What are a refire and a remake?
cards.back: A dish cooked again, or rebuilt, because it came back from the table or failed the check at the pass; it is fired first, ahead of the queue.

cards.front: How does a server bring a problem to the pass?
cards.back: Calmly and plainly: table, seat, dish, what is wrong and what the guest would like. Blame waits until after service.

cards.front: How is a guest's allergy plate handled at the pass and by the kitchen?
cards.back: Flagged on the ticket, checked against it with the kitchen, and carried separately, alone, straight to the right seat.

cards.front: At Brennan's, who clears a guest's dietary needs?
cards.back: The kitchen, every time. The server writes the needs on the ticket, flags it and tells the captain, and the kitchen says what a dish can do.

questions.q: In a restaurant kitchen, what is the pass?
questions.answer: The counter where plates are checked and sent
distractors: The walk-in cold room where stock is kept
The station that cooks the fish to order
The board that lists the dishes that have run out
questions.why: The pass is the kitchen's last checkpoint: every plate crosses it, and is checked there, before it reaches a guest.

questions.q: Which of these jobs belongs to the expediter?
questions.answer: Firing each course when the table is ready
distractors: Washing the pots, pans and plates for the line
Pouring and decanting the wine at the table
Breaking down meat and poultry for the stations
questions.why: The expediter owns the tickets: reading them, firing courses, calling for plates and checking each one. The others belong to the plongeur, sommelier and boucher.

questions.q: A steak takes twelve minutes with its rest and the fish takes six. How does the expediter time them?
questions.answer: Fire the steak first, the fish six minutes later
distractors: Fire both together and hold the fish under the lamp
Fire the fish first, then the steak when it is up
Send each plate out as soon as it is ready
questions.why: Counting back from the slowest dish brings every plate to the pass at the same moment, so the table eats together and nothing waits.

questions.q: A plate has sat at the pass long enough for its sauce to form a skin. What happens?
questions.answer: It goes back for fresh
distractors: A server runs it out at once
The expediter wipes the skin away
It goes out with an apology
questions.why: Hot food goes out hot and sauces fresh; a plate that has died under the lamp reaches the guest worse than the kitchen made it.

questions.q: Why does a server keep the thumb flat at the outer edge, never across the rim?
questions.answer: The cook has just wiped it clean
distractors: The rim is the hottest part
It stops the sauce from moving
The kitchen counts plates by the rim
questions.why: The rim frames the plate; a thumbprint there undoes the cook's last wipe in front of the guest.

questions.q: What should a server bring to the pass when collecting a table's plates?
questions.answer: Free hands and the seat numbers
distractors: A cloth to wipe each rim on the way out
A tray to stack the whole table's plates
A tray of clean glasses for the table
questions.why: Free hands carry the plates at once, and seat numbers put each plate in front of the right guest without asking who had what.

questions.q: A guest's steak is overcooked. How does the server bring it to the pass?
questions.answer: Calmly: table, seat, dish, fault, guest's wish
distractors: Loudly, so the grill cook hears every word of it
Quietly, by fixing it out in the dining room
Later, once the rest of the table has finished eating
questions.why: Plain detail lets the expediter fire the replacement at once and decide on the rest of the table; blame waits until after service.

questions.q: Once the kitchen has checked a guest's allergy plate against the ticket, how does it leave the pass?
questions.answer: Carried alone, straight to the guest's seat
distractors: Stacked with the table's other plates
Run by whoever is free, with no word about the flag
Held under the lamp until the table is ready
questions.why: Carried separately, the plate is far less likely to be swapped or touched by another; the kitchen checks it against the ticket at the pass first.

questions.q: At Brennan's, who has the final word on what a dish can do for a guest's dietary needs?
questions.answer: The kitchen
distractors: The server
The captain
The manager on duty
questions.why: The house guide is plain: write it on the ticket, flag it, tell the captain, and let the kitchen clear every choice.
